title: Parks Committee
overview: The Village of Kronenwetter Parks Committee held its August 3rd meeting to discuss village communications about parks, additional ideas for park improvements including a second dog park, disc golf course, water access points, and trail benches, as well as reviewing a first draft of a 2026-2036 Capital Improvements Program budget. The committee reached broad consensus to delay the September 12 Bush Cook Park fun run/walk fundraiser due to inadequate planning, and agreed to each bring their top three park priorities to the next meeting to help focus the committee's direction and budget requests.

discussions.body: The chair noted one name correction had already been provided to staff. A motion was made by Patty and seconded by Elizabeth to approve the minutes with that correction. There was no further discussion and the motion carried 6-0.

Chair Mishka raised the item after a Facebook post showed a resident was unaware of public park amenities near Municipal Center Park. The committee reviewed the village website live and found outdated information, including a listing for volleyball courts where no net exists. Members suggested linking existing YouTube park videos directly to each park's page, adding maps of walking trails, and including information about the Kronenwetter and Leather Camp forest management units. Village Administrator Jim suggested a 'one park a month' social media highlight campaign beginning in spring 2027, tying park communications to the budget process to keep residents informed of planned enhancements.

discussions.item: Additional Ideas for Other Park Land and Related Village Property
discussions.body: Committee member Tim presented several ideas: a second dog park at Norm Klaas Park (already listed as medium priority in the capital improvements plan), a disc golf course at the 33-acre Well Head Park (with security camera concerns raised for the wellhead facility), water access/boat launch points at Gardner Park and the end of Nelson Road, and benches along walking trails potentially funded through memorial donations or Eagle Scout projects. The Village Administrator urged the committee to prioritize all ideas rather than presenting them piecemeal to the board, emphasizing laser focus on Bush Cook Park for 2027 and recommending members each bring their personal top three major priorities to the next meeting. Staff noted the 2025 Outdoor Recreation Plan already includes prioritized projects with cost estimates that should serve as a starting point.

discussions.item: 2026-2036 Capital Improvements Program Budget First Draft
discussions.body: Village Finance Director John Jacobs presented the first-ever long-range CIP document for the village, which lists projects across all departments including every park. He explained that only 2027 items will be formally adopted by the board in November, while outer years remain a living planning document. Jacobs noted the village currently has roughly 80% of its borrowing capacity available and discussed debt structuring strategies to smooth tax impacts. The $200,000 listed for Bush Cook Park in 2027 is expected to come from donations, and the Administrator stressed the committee must make a strong case to the board to supplement any funding gap. Members were encouraged to share the CIP document with neighbors to build community support.

discussions.item: September 12, 2026 Bush Cook Park 5K Run/Walk Fundraiser Event
discussions.body: Village Administrator Jim raised significant concerns about the September 12th date, noting police officers are scheduled a year in advance and would require overtime, a large portion of fire volunteers would be unavailable that weekend due to commitments in the Fox Valley, and no detailed operational plan had been presented to the committee. A member also noted September 12th is adjacent to the 9/11 anniversary, which felt inappropriate for a fundraising event. The committee broadly agreed the event should be delayed, with the Administrator planning to contact Trustee Aaron Myszka, who had organized the effort, to discuss postponing to spring 2027, potentially tying a fun run to a ribbon-cutting celebration if the playground equipment is funded and installed.

title: Community Life, Infrastructure and Public Property (CLIPP) Committee Meeting
overview: The Village of Kronenwetter's CLIPP Committee met on August 3, 2026, taking action on four items: approving July meeting minutes, recommending the county maintain a four-way stop at County Highway XX and Teraboni Drive, rescinding the Oak Wilt ordinance and reimbursement policy, and recommending a one-year moratorium on data center development to the Village Board. The committee also received a first look at the village's inaugural 2027–2036 Capital Improvement Program, a significant planning milestone for a village that had previously operated without any multi-year capital plan.

discussions.body: Two speakers addressed the committee. Trustee Dan Lesniak, speaking as a resident and in his role as Plan Commission Chair, urged the committee to recommend retaining the four-way stop at XX/Teraboni for public safety, and encouraged the committee to move forward with a data center moratorium so the Plan Commission can craft appropriate regulations. No other public speakers came forward.

discussions.item: Approval of July 6 Committee Meeting Minutes
discussions.body: Minutes were moved and seconded with no discussion. The committee approved them 4-0.

The police chief reported approximately 800 calls for service in July, noting an anecdotal spike in domestic violence incidents; one arrest resulted in 10 felony and 3 misdemeanor charges with a $50,000 cash bond. The fire chief reported the department was awarded a WPS Rewarding Responders grant to purchase a new thermal imaging camera and noted an ISO audit scheduled for the following day. The public works/utilities director reported ongoing communication with the FBI and EPA regarding cybersecurity threats to municipal water systems nationally, noting some systems had been hacked due to lack of passwords, and stated Kronenwetter has security measures in place. The complaint log showed seven complaints year-to-date, with staff noting the incoming new community development director starting Thursday would help resume normal enforcement activity.

discussions.item: Four-Way Stop at County Highway XX and Teraboni Drive
discussions.body: Greg presented an email from Marathon County indicating the county's traffic study supports retaining a four-way stop at the intersection, though the county wanted the village's input before a Thursday committee meeting. One committee member noted personal daily use of the intersection and observed it was 'much better' as a four-way stop. The committee voted 4-0 to recommend to the county that the four-way stop be retained, with the understanding that the county retains jurisdiction and makes the final decision.

discussions.item: Oak Wilt Ordinance Review and Rescission
discussions.body: Greg presented proposed changes to the village's Oak Wilt ordinance, noting the village has no tree inspector on staff or under contract, no longer has grant funding to assist residents with removal costs, and that Oak Wilt has spread so widely across Wisconsin that strict local enforcement is impractical. The committee debated village liability and discussed whether maintaining an unenforceable ordinance created risk. The consensus was that without the funding mechanism or tree inspector, the ordinance and associated reimbursement policy should be rescinded, with residents referred to the DNR. The committee voted 4-0 to rescind both the Oak Wilt ordinance and the reimbursement policy.

A committee member introduced the resolution, describing concerns about the massive scale of data centers, their extraordinary water consumption, and the village's existing water capacity challenges. Jim noted he had spoken with a director at Wausau/Marathon County who is developing ordinance language to define and restrict data centers, and offered to share that language with relevant boards. One member noted AI data centers generate strong community opposition. A minor drafting error was caught — the resolution referred to 'the cities' rather than 'the village' — which staff agreed to correct. The committee voted 4-0 to recommend the moratorium resolution directly to the Village Board for approval.

Greg reported that a minimum cost estimate for a new trail in Kronenwetter would be at least $600,000 for construction alone, not including wetlands, culverts, or engineering. The county indicated it would not contribute financially. The committee generally agreed that trail planning should be referred to the Parks Committee for prioritization, and that trail construction is likely most cost-effective when bundled with road projects rather than as standalone projects. A member with prior experience at the Village of Weston noted that trail paths along county roads in that area were historically funded by county and state dollars, not village funds, suggesting a similar approach could apply here if a future connector road is built.

Finance Director John presented the village's first-ever 10-year Capital Improvement Program, noting the village had previously operated entirely year-to-year with no long-term capital plan. The current draft covers approximately $4.3 million in priority projects across departments, with roughly $1.2 million remaining from a 2024 general obligation borrowing and a possible new GO borrowing of approximately $1.7 million. Major infrastructure items include Maple Ridge Road engineering and reconstruction, Martin Road reconstruction (flagged by a committee member as the village's worst road and priority given heavy resident use of the compost site), sewer lift station panel upgrades and SCADA system, a new water tower and well, and deferred municipal center maintenance including boiler and roofing. The fire department noted rescue truck number 6 would need to be ordered well before its 2029 scheduled replacement due to 3-4 year delivery timelines. The document was presented as a living, versioned working document to be refined through August, September, and October ahead of November budget adoption.

Dan Lesniak (816 Spring Road), a village trustee and Plan Commission Chair, spoke in favor of retaining the four-way stop at XX/Teraboni for public safety and encouraged the committee to advance the data center moratorium so the Plan Commission can develop appropriate regulations. No other members of the public spoke.

title: Community Development Authority
committee: Community Development Authority, Village of Weston
overview: The Village of Weston Community Development Authority held a brief meeting on the closing of TIF District No. 1, which added $354 million in assessed value since 1998 and accumulated $95.7 million in increment over its life. The CDA voted unanimously to redeem the outstanding 2017A lease revenue bonds early, paying off debt ahead of the 2031 schedule. The board also received an update on TIF District No. 2, which carries a $841,000 deficit and is expected to close within a few years, and discussed the future role of the CDA itself.

discussions.body: A motion to approve the minutes was made by Lisa and seconded by Ted. The motion passed unanimously with no discussion.

Staff (identified as Jessica) reported that TIF District No. 1, open since 1998, has recovered all costs and is ready to close. The TIF added $354 million in assessed value, incurred $86 million in project costs, and collected $95.7 million in total increment. Members asked whether sufficient funds exist to call the outstanding debt; Jessica confirmed they do. Staff noted that closing the TIF will shift the assessed value to the general tax roll, likely producing a significant tax rate reduction for village residents, and that the village expects to be allowed to increase its levy by approximately $400,000. Approximately $200,000 in administration cost allocations will also return to the general fund.

Jessica reported that TIF District No. 2, created in 2004 around Schofield Avenue, carries a $841,000 deficit following a large state-mandated value reduction last year. The TIF has no remaining debt, only the deficit to repay through ongoing increment. No new projects or expenditures are planned; the district is expected to close before its 2031 deadline. Members also briefly discussed the possibility of future TIFs, including a potential small district near Highway J, but staff noted no formal proposal exists and that changes to state TIF law are still evolving.

discussions.item: Approval of Resolution Authorizing Redemption of CDA Lease Revenue Bonds Series 2017A
discussions.body: The board voted on a resolution to call and redeem the outstanding CDA lease revenue bonds (Series 2017A, dated July 13, 2017), paying bondholders in full with interest rather than continuing payments through 2031. A member identified as Hogan moved approval and Mark seconded. The motion passed unanimously.

Members and staff discussed whether the CDA should continue to exist once TIF 2 closes, noting it has no debt to administer and has not conducted business visits since 2018. Staff suggested bringing the question of disbanding or repurposing the CDA to the full Village Board for direction, and a member asked staff to add it to the board's next monthly agenda. Members noted the CDA is established by ordinance, so any dissolution would require a formal ordinance change.

overview: The Kronenwetter Village Board held its July 27, 2026 meeting and approved several significant items including a rezoning of Marathon County Highway Department property from B3SF and AR to M2 General Industrial, a Bushka Park 5K run/walk fundraiser for September 12, matching a $5,000 parks grant, and multiple budget amendments. The board also discussed the Quasquerot interchange opportunity and gave consensus to move forward on a zero-lot line ordinance change.

discussions.body: Keefe Wolkowski spoke in favor of the zero-lot line concept, noting he first brought it to the Planning Commission about two years ago. He explained that the proposal involves 60-foot-wide lots that would allow twin-home ownership, with each owner holding their half, and cited adoption by Rothschild, Weston, and Marshfield. He noted Gary Gurn and Timberidge Builders are interested in a mixed twin-home and single-family development in Kronenwetter.

Resident Guy Fredel made an extended argument for keeping the Quasquerot interchange in the Wausau MPO's long-range transportation plan, noting that Duane Gaau (MPO chairperson) had written to President Joling asking for the village's position. Fredel highlighted that federal interchange standards have been reduced from seven criteria to two, that state law requires Wisconsin to cover 100% of costs if a federal waiver is needed, and that two state representatives had expressed interest in funding it in the next budget cycle. He argued safety concerns on the current I-39 northbound ramp support the interchange.

Finance Director John James reported the village is at roughly 54% of revenues collected and 43% of expenditures spent at the six-month mark, which he characterized as healthy overall. He flagged three areas of concern: the village attorney budget is $10,000 over budget due to a personnel investigation with more invoices expected; the municipal building is at 53% spent due to unexpected repairs from deferred maintenance; and the garbage/recycling budget is at 54% spent due to a diesel fuel surcharge triggered when prices exceed $4 per contract. James indicated the $60,000 contingency reserve would be used to address overages via future budget amendments through APC and the board.

Finance Director James presented a timetable calling for the CIP budget review to begin at the August 3rd CLIP committee meeting, with two budget workshops planned for October 19 and 20, with the October 19 meeting starting earlier in the afternoon to avoid conflicting with Planning Commission. Final budget adoption is targeted for the November 9 board meeting. Trustees were encouraged to attend any committee budget meetings and to raise questions early so the final adoption meeting would be largely settled.

discussions.item: Item K: Rezoning - Marathon County Highway Facility
discussions.body: Dan Joling reported the Planning Commission, after completing its discussion today following a storm-interrupted meeting the prior Monday, unanimously found all six required criteria were met and recommended approval of the rezoning of 25.247 acres from B3SF and AR to M2 General Industrial for the Marathon County Highway Department facility. Marathon County Highway Commissioner Kevin Lee clarified that the facility's water plan involves three components: the main building connected to village sewer and water, a private well for brine-making (a high-volume use that does not enter the sewer), and a private well for the wash bay with metered sewer discharge. The board approved the rezoning 7-0.

discussions.item: Item N: Twin-Home Zero-Lot Line Ordinance - Planning Commission Guidance
discussions.body: Planning Commission representative Dan [Joling] explained the commission was seeking board consensus to proceed with drafting ordinance changes to allow zero-lot line twin-home lots, following a prior recommendation that did not advance. Multiple trustees expressed support, with one noting the previous failure was partly due to misperceptions that these would be low-income rentals, when in fact units sell for approximately $400,000 per side. The board reached consensus to direct staff and the Planning Commission to gather ordinances from neighboring communities and draft language for a public hearing and future board approval. No formal vote was taken.

discussions.item: Item O: Bushka Park 5K Run/Walk Fundraiser
discussions.body: Parks Committee Chair Erin Mishka presented a plan for a September 12, 2026 fundraiser event featuring both a 5K and a 3K route through Bushka Park, Towering Pines Park, and Civil Park, ending at Relocation Public Needary whose owner agreed to host participants and donate a percentage of sales to the Bushka Park project. President Joling volunteered to provide music. Chief McEul reviewed the routes and approved the intersections plan. The board approved the event unanimously on a voice vote.

discussions.item: Item P: Wausau Marathon County Parks and Recreation Foundation Grant Match
discussions.body: Mishka reported the village was awarded a $5,000 grant from the Wausau Marathon County Parks and Recreation Foundation, with the foundation expressing a preference (not a requirement) for a $5,000 municipal match. Finance Director James said the match would be moved from the existing general fund parks budget into a dedicated park fund for transparency, with a formal budget amendment to come through APC in August. The board approved the $5,000 match 7-0, with trustees noting that matching demonstrates community investment and positions the village well for future grant applications.

discussions.body: The board considered a previously approved $14,815 addition for a bathroom on the police side of the new municipal garage, requiring a formal budget amendment. The amendment adds the cost to the capital projects fund. Trustee Lesniak moved and Trustee Solheim seconded; the board approved 7-0.

The board approved the sealing contract 7-0 and then approved Budget Amendment #4 allocating the $37,884 across capital projects fund and TID areas 7-0. Trustee Mishka noted participants in a recent village bike event particularly enjoyed the paths being maintained.

Resident Guy Fredel distributed materials and made an extended argument urging the board to reaffirm support for the Quasquerot interchange in the Wausau MPO long-range transportation plan, citing reduced federal standards, potential state funding, and economic impact projections of 1,200 jobs and $120 million in new valuation.

title: Environmental Resources Committee - Educational Meeting
overview: The Marathon County Environmental Resources Committee held a special educational meeting with no votes taken, featuring conservation staff introductions and program updates, followed by background on proposed animal waste ordinance changes. Four public commenters addressed concerns about manure spreading regulations, wind turbine development, and water quality, while staff presented on municipal wellhead protection successes in Athens and Rib Mountain, a walleye telemetry study on the Big Eau Pleine, and shoreline restoration projects.

discussions.item: Public Comment - Manure Ordinance and Agriculture Regulations
discussions.body: Christine Cafer (Town of McMillan) questioned where the other 72% of phosphorus load in the Wisconsin River basin originates beyond Marathon County's 28%, raised concerns about storage cost burdens on farms without facilities, and asked the committee to identify scientific evidence that additional county regulations will produce measurable improvements beyond existing state programs. Dean Beck, a member of the animal waste task force representing eastern Marathon County, warned that the proposed ordinance focuses only on animal waste while commercial fertilizer used by crop farmers contains equally significant phosphorus and nitrogen, potentially undermining the ordinance's water quality goals. Pat Saha (Town of Repro), also on the task force, expressed general support for a February-March winter spreading ban and for requiring nutrient management plans for all farmers, and shared a positive personal experience installing buffer strips that improved water quality without reducing yield.

discussions.item: Public Comment - Hub City Wind and Utility-Scale Wind Development
discussions.body: Nikki Catrell (Town of Brighton) asked the committee to place utility-scale wind development on a future agenda and to recommend the county board adopt a temporary moratorium while evaluating whether current ordinances adequately address projects of this scale. She argued that modern turbines are dramatically larger than those that shaped existing regulations and cited a Wisconsin Badger Hollow Wind proceeding in which independent audiologist Dr. Jerry Punch from Michigan State University found a developer's acoustic analysis fundamentally inadequate, concluding that independent expert review is necessary before irreversible decisions are made. She drew a parallel to the committee's planned August consideration of a moratorium on data centers, arguing the same principle should apply to wind development.

discussions.item: Conservation Staff Introductions and Program Overview
discussions.body: Conservation staff — Matt Reking, Ken Pazorski (who announced his retirement after 35 years), Kirk Lane, Brooke Benick, Caleb Armstrong, and Jared Mdd — each described their program areas including animal waste ordinance administration, livestock licensing, farmland preservation, nutrient management training, managed grazing, the EPIC producer group, youth education, and water resources. Staff noted the team has over 130 combined years of experience across eight conservationists. A committee member asked about anaerobic digesters, and staff clarified that digesters in Marathon County are all on CAFO farms regulated by the state DNR, so the county is not directly involved.

discussions.item: Wisconsin Land and Water Training Debrief
discussions.body: Staff invited committee members to share takeaways from a Wisconsin Land and Water training held in Merrill approximately six weeks prior. One committee member highlighted learning about Lincoln County's culvert fish passage assessment and the technical complexity of manure spill response. Staff noted that Marathon County statistically has the fifth most manure spills in Wisconsin. The session was informal and conversational, with no formal action.

discussions.item: Municipal Wellhead Protection Updates - Athens, Rib Mountain, Hatley
discussions.body: Staff described the completed Athens project, where 30 acres nearest municipal wells were converted to prairie and 30 acres to pasture, eliminating row-crop nutrient applications near wells with increasing nitrates. The private landowner received a higher rental payment than under row crops. Staff reported Athens residents have embraced the prairie on social media and the village reached out this week requesting more prairie. A similar project is underway in Rib Mountain adjacent to Rib Mountain State Park and Depkey Park on County Road N, with multiple funding sources stacked to make the project a win for all parties. Staff also reported early-stage outreach to the Village of Hatley, which has only one municipal well with nitrates already above 7 mg/L and rising, serving a population of about 500 with an average age of 33.

discussions.item: Big Eau Pleine Walleye Acoustic Telemetry Fish Movement Study
discussions.body: Jared Mdd presented updates on a 10-year walleye tagging study initiated through a surface water grant that also funded replacement of the Big Eau Pleine aeration system (originally installed in 1980). In year one, 30 walleye were tagged; 8 were caught by anglers, 7 were harvested but all tags returned and recycled. In year two, 12 additional tags were purchased and 7 new fish tagged. Receivers are placed throughout the flowage to track fish movement every 30 seconds via acoustic pings. Staff noted 4 receivers are currently missing, likely lost during spring ice breakup, and DNR divers will search for them this fall. One fish passed through Moon Dam and is believed to be in Lake Dubay.

discussions.item: Animal Waste Ordinance Proposed Changes Overview
discussions.body: Staff briefly reviewed proposed ordinance changes that have been under discussion for approximately eight months to a year, given time constraints. Key proposals include: requiring a nutrient management plan or a winter spreading permit for anyone applying liquid manure in winter, with setbacks from water bodies and sensitive areas; and a February-March liquid manure spreading ban for farms at approximately 300 animal units (roughly 150 milk cows and 150 young stock) or greater. CAFO operations at 1,000 animal units or greater are already subject to these requirements under state law. Staff noted the animal waste ordinance work group of approximately 25 stakeholders — including farmers, water resource professionals, and seed dealers — has been involved in developing these proposals. The meeting ended before a full discussion could occur due to time constraints.

publicComment: Four speakers offered public comment. Christine Cafer (Town of McMillan) raised concerns about the cost burden of manure storage facilities, questioned the scientific basis for county regulations beyond existing state programs, and asked where the other 72% of Wisconsin River phosphorus load originates. Nikki Catrell (Town of Brighton) requested the committee place utility-scale wind development on a future agenda and consider a temporary moratorium, citing concerns about outdated ordinances and the need for independent acoustic review, analogous to the planned data center moratorium. Dean Beck (County East), a member of the animal waste task force, warned that excluding crop farmers using commercial fertilizer from the ordinance would undermine phosphorus reduction goals. Pat Saha (Town of Repro), also on the task force, expressed support for the February-March winter spreading ban, mandatory nutrient management plans, and buffer strips, sharing a positive personal experience with buffers on his own farm.

overview: The Village of Weston Finance and Human Resources Committee met on Monday, July 21, 2025, taking action on several items including approving a renewed Cintas uniform agreement, approving related employee policy handbook changes, extending the village's audit contract with Hawkins Ash for 2026, acknowledging the 2025 final audit report, and approving the 2027 budget process calendar with joint Finance/HR and board meetings. The meeting also included a substantive discussion about staff morale, the annual exit interview report, and an introduction of an ethics policy review process referred from the board of trustees.

discussions.body: One member of the public, Jim, spoke on three topics: opposition to removing the legal detail from Finance and HR Committee packets, requesting to comment during the Cintas contract discussion given his two decades of experience with uniform contracts, and criticizing the exit interview report for including staff opinions rather than factual employee interview data. The chair allowed Jim to speak during the Cintas agenda item without objection from the committee.

discussions.item: June Budget Status Report and TIF Reports (Items 5-7)
discussions.body: A committee member asked Finance Director Jessica about the aquatic center revenue covering 50.42% of expenditures to date, and Jessica explained season pass sales in June account for a large portion of revenue. She noted the aquatic center receives $40,000 in property tax levy and $40,000 in room tax annually, and that balancing it is a year-to-year struggle. Items 5, 6, and 7 were acknowledged together by motion.

Staff reported three transitions in the past six months. It was noted that a previously full-time deputy clerk position was split into two part-time positions successfully, reducing benefit costs. An engineering tech (RAS) was recently brought on, and two positions — deputy clerk/administrative assistant and utility operator/maintainer — were currently posted for recruitment.

HR staff Jamie presented the report, noting only one exit interview was completed and that for confidentiality reasons no specific recommendations were attributed to that individual. The report included commentary about increasing negativity and unconstructive criticism affecting staff morale, which generated significant discussion. A committee member argued the win of a 7.5% turnover rate — below public sector benchmarks — was being overshadowed by the opinion-laden portion of the report and suggested separating the factual turnover data from the morale discussion, making the latter a standing agenda item. Mark (identified in discussion as a village official present) stated he personally refuses to respond to criticism in outside media and expressed support for staff. A department director spoke about the difficulty staff face being identified in public while wearing village shirts and receiving negative comments. Jamie defended including the morale content as reflective of themes heard more broadly, not just from the one exit interview, noting it could be a leading indicator if turnover worsens. The committee agreed to add a standing item for August on how the committee can better support staff, and one member proposed adding encomiums as a standing agenda item at board meetings. The motion to acknowledge the report passed with one opposed vote.

Public commenter Jim, who was invited to speak, shared detailed experience with uniform contracts, recommending the village negotiate seasonal garment rates to avoid makeup charges, standardize garment types to reduce costs (noting stretchy jeans cost four times standard pants), and consider an allowance model where employees pay the difference for premium options. DPW Director Michael explained the current contract uses Omnia Partners government pricing locking rates for 36 months, that Cintas would not go below a 36-month term, and that a minimum weekly charge of approximately $45 (50% of current ~$92/week bill) would still be met even if some employees opted out. He noted communication and weekly check-ins with the Cintas driver have improved. The committee discussed the opt-out hybrid model, employee satisfaction, female employees having difficulty finding well-fitting garments, and the January 1 start date for annual selections. The committee recommended approval of the Cintas uniform agreement renewal to the board of trustees.

The committee discussed amendments to Chapter 5 (job classification and compensation, clothing and equipment loans) and Chapter 10 (appearance) of the personnel policies handbook to reflect the new hybrid uniform program — allowing employees to either use Cintas or receive a $500 clothing allowance, compared to the current $300 reimbursement. Staff confirmed this was essentially codifying the agreement approved in Item 10. The committee recommended approval of the policy amendments to the board of trustees.

Finance Director Jessica presented a proposal from Hawkins Ash to continue as the village's auditor for the 2026 audit at a cost of $41,105. She noted this is lower than the $43,000–$46,000 proposals received from other firms during the last RFP process (for the 2025 audit), and that retaining Hawkins Ash is beneficial because of their familiarity with the village's TIF districts and existing work papers. The committee recommended approval of the one-year extension to the board of trustees.

Finance Director Jessica presented the final 2025 audit report from Hawkins Ash, noting she had included a memo summarizing the highlights to make the voluminous document more accessible. A committee member appreciated the memo. The committee acknowledged the final audit report without significant discussion.

Finance Director Amy (or Jessica) presented a proposed budget calendar, noting that the September 7 meeting date falls on Labor Day and should be moved to Tuesday, September 8. The committee discussed whether Finance and HR should hold joint meetings with the full board of trustees throughout the budget process or focus narrowly on wages and benefits as in prior years. Two committee members expressed preference for participating in the full budget process. The motion to approve the calendar and hold joint meetings with the board was approved unanimously.

discussions.item: Ethics Function Referral from Board of Trustees (Item 15)
discussions.body: The chair introduced this item, explaining that after raising the concept at the last board of trustees meeting, the board referred the task of developing a potential ethics process to the Finance and HR Committee. The chair noted the current ethics policy (page 226 of the packet) routes violations to a department director or administrator, and that the committee would explore whether to build upon, amend, or replace it. A committee member suggested a citizen-based body similar to the police and fire commission, with the chair agreeing that was a possibility worth considering. The chair noted the committee may grow from four to six members after that evening's board of trustees meeting and wanted to wait for that input before going deeper. Staff were asked to gather sample ethics policies from comparable municipalities for the August meeting discussion.

Finally, he criticized the exit interview report for including staff opinions rather than factual interview data and suggested the committee hold a listening session for staff to share thoughts directly.

overview: The Weston Village Board of Trustees held a wide-ranging meeting covering several significant decisions, most notably approving the Mountain Bay Metropolitan Police Department building contract with 8 Pine Inc. for $6.7 million — coming in under a $7 million budget — and receiving a detailed presentation from DC Everest school district leaders on long-range facility planning that could include a $81–94 million referendum in April 2027. The board also discussed SAFER fire staffing, public works challenges including asbestos pipe replacement and utility operator turnover, and various committee reports.

discussions.body: Jim Pinsel addressed the board on three topics: (1) strong opposition to removing legal details from the Finance and HR Committee's monthly review, arguing it enables 'swampy underhanded backroom deals' and citing $10,000 in legal fees he said were used to avoid public records disclosure; (2) support for the police department building but urging that the $362,354.32 in returned EMPD funds be exclusively earmarked to reduce borrowing for the new building; and (3) a call for the board to set 2027 budget goals including fully funding the fire department and minimizing property taxes.

discussions.item: DC Everest Long-Range Facility Planning Presentation
discussions.body: Superintendent Dr. Casey Nye and Assistant Superintendent Dr. Kelly Strike presented DC Everest's long-range facility plan, which involves decommissioning the 75-year-old junior high, moving 8th graders to the middle school (creating a 6–8 building) and 9th graders to the high school (creating a 9–12 building), with an estimated cost of $81–94 million plus potential additional costs if a new aquatics facility is added. The district is targeting an April 2027 referendum, noting that current enrollment has declined from about 5,900 five years ago to 5,730, and that the 2018 referendum passed with roughly 70.8% approval. Trustees asked about the operational costs of retaining the junior high structure partially, staffing reductions (attrition-based, no planned layoffs), the age of other facilities, and the potential pool project near GTCC. Dr. Nye acknowledged the pool decision is exploratory and that community partnership conversations are ongoing.

discussions.item: Mountain Bay Metro Police Department Bid Results (Item 54)
discussions.body: Chief Mark Kern presented bid results for the new Mountain Bay Metropolitan Police Department building: the base bid from contractor 8 Pine Inc. came in at $6,390,100, with the total project including fiber optic line, lockers, furniture, and security estimated at $6.7 million — under the $7 million budget. Five bid alternatives were considered; three were eliminated. The approximately 26,000 sq. ft. building includes a 13-squad garage expandable during adverse weather. Trustee Katrina Clark expressed disappointment at the process that led to needing a new building, saying she felt misled when the merger was approved after being told existing facilities were adequate; Chief Kern took personal responsibility, apologizing to the board. Finance administrator Ryan noted an intergovernmental agreement with Rothschild must be finalized in August before the contract with 8 Pine can be signed; 8 Pine indicated it could begin construction by end of September. Weston's share is approximately $4,355,000 (65%), with Rothschild covering 35%. The board voted unanimously 7-0 to approve the contract.

Trustee Barbara Ermeling reported the committee discussed the Cintas agreement and an annual exit interview report showing 7.5% village-wide staff turnover, which she characterized as a strong result for a public entity. The committee also discussed ways elected officials can show appreciation to staff, with follow-up planned for August.

Director Michael reported the Alderson-Gelnik roundabout is progressing with curb and gutter poured and sidewalk work beginning; utility pole removal was delayed until after the World Cup finale due to telecom contract restrictions. A utility operator gave two-week notice — the third consecutive year of turnover in that position around the one-year mark — raising concerns about operational impact and training burden. Discussion also covered the asbestos pipe replacement program (10 miles in the village, with a grant being pursued), street lighting gaps near the river and along Score Avenue to campus, and the long-term future of the bridge over the Oclair River on Ross Avenue. Trustees also discussed the planned Ross Avenue and Camp Phillips roundabout, driven by crash analysis and a traffic study showing the intersection trending toward level-of-service F by 2034.

Village President Maloney and others briefly discussed the SAFER board's approval of adding three staff for 2027, which the board indicated they have comfort funding via TIF district closure revenue without a referendum. Maloney expressed the need for a longer-term staffing plan — potentially adding two more in year two and three more in year three — to be discussed during budget season, noting the public's rejection of the fire fee referendum signaled they do not want another referendum approach.

Key outcomes included approving a recommendation to the village board to hold a September 12 Bushka Park 5K/3K run-walk as an official village event, approving a motion to ask the board for a $5,000 matching grant, and declining a $2,000 funding request for a planned August 21 concert fundraiser, which was subsequently postponed to spring 2027.

discussions.body: A motion was made by committee member Patty to approve the June 29, 2026 Parks Committee meeting minutes, seconded by Elizabeth. The motion carried unanimously on a voice vote.

discussions.item: Bushka Park Renovation Project Grant Update
discussions.body: Staff reported that three grants were submitted, including one to WASOW (outcome pending) and the Marathon County Parks and Recreation Foundation Fund grant for which the village received $5,000. A committee member asked for clarification on whether $100,000 was the total grant pool or the eligibility cap. Staff noted they had a call in with WASOW and expected to hear back. A motion was made by Patty and seconded by another member to recommend the village board approve a $5,000 match to the received grant; the motion carried 7-0.

The committee conducted a lengthy park-by-park review of Municipal Park, Towering Pines, Friendship Park, Bushka Park, and Seville Park. Recurring themes across all parks included failing ADA accessibility (notably only one handicap swing in the village, which is itself inaccessible), aging playground equipment (15-20 years old), vandalism of bathrooms, poorly maintained Little Free Libraries, signage issues, and underuse of facilities. Staff member Greg confirmed budget constraints with only three part-time parks staff and five full-time streets staff covering seven parks. The committee directed staff to compile a prioritized list with rough cost estimates for the next meeting, and noted that a full assessment cannot be completed until all parks are reviewed. ADA compliance was identified as a high-priority cross-park issue.

discussions.item: August 21, 2026 Concert at Towering Pines Fundraiser Event
discussions.body: Committee member Patty presented a plan for a fundraiser concert featuring donated band Living River on August 21, with proposed amenities including a bounce house, petting zoo, face painting, and free food funded by a $2,000 village board allocation from the community events budget. Trustees Mishka and Lesniak expressed concern about using village funds for a fundraising event with uncertain returns, and about event redundancy given National Night Out and the planned 5K. A motion by Patty for up to $2,000 from the village board was seconded for discussion purposes; the motion failed with only Patty voting yes. Following the failed vote, Patty indicated she would cancel the August 21 event and look at rescheduling to spring 2027.

Committee member Aaron presented a detailed plan for a 5K/3K run-walk starting at Bushka Park, passing through Towering Pines, and ending at Relocation Public Eatery, with music provided by a musician personally sponsored by Village President Dan Joling. Police Chief Terry McEwen confirmed police support for road closures. Relocation owner Jackie Fisher approved the event and proposed raffle baskets, 50/50 drawings, and potentially donating a percentage of food and drink sales. discussions.item: FEMA Declaration and Community Assistance Update
discussions.body: Sarah, the county's Public Information Officer, presented a detailed update on FEMA and SBA disaster assistance following the April 13–23, 2026 severe storms, tornadoes, and flooding. She reported that as of July 15, 24 Marathon County residents had filed FEMA individual assistance applications, with four filed the previous day. A FEMA Disaster Recovery Center opened July 14 at the Town of Ringle Municipal Center (Monday–Friday, 1–7 p.m.), and an SBA Business Recovery Center opened July 13 at the Marathon County Public Library Wausau headquarters (Monday–Friday, 9 a.m.–4:30 p.m.). A new recovery resource page was also launched at marathoncounty.gov/ia.

Sarah explained that while Marathon County was approved for individual assistance, it was denied for FEMA public assistance — which covers governmental costs such as debris removal, road repairs, and public infrastructure — along with Bayfield, Manitowoc, and Racine counties. The per-capita damage threshold for Marathon County was $670,743.18, but documented damages from the April storms totaled only approximately $271,000. County staff reviewed whether any additional damages had been missed and concluded they had not; therefore, the county informed Wisconsin Emergency Management it would not pursue an appeal. Gibbs emphasized to committee members that the public assistance denial does not affect individuals' ability to apply for individual assistance.

discussions.item: Insurance Settlements and Town of Ringle Property Questions
discussions.body: Supervisor Robinson asked about the status of insurance company settlements for homes in the Town of Ringle that may need to be demolished, raising concerns about deadlines and potential need for the county to extend deadlines or forgive fees. Gibbs responded that he had not received a follow-up from Ringle representatives but pledged to reach out, noting that Sarah had attended a recent Ringle board meeting on these topics. He mentioned that free legal consultation through the State Bar of Wisconsin and resources from the State Commission on Insurance had been made available to affected residents, and that the Town of Ringle was also exploring whether to issue raze orders for disputed properties.

Gibbs presented the item on behalf of Vice Chair Boots, who had to leave to catch a flight. He asked committee members whether anything was missing from the strategic plan survey included in their packets. Supervisor Arseth asked whether the survey would be available online; Gibbs confirmed it would be sent to county board members as a link-based online survey, similar to the work plan ranking process. No content gaps were identified by members present. Gibbs noted a separate public input process would be used.

discussions.item: Proposed Revisions to Chapter 41 Elections - CLIP Committee
discussions.body: The board discussed three options for handling election-related ordinance revisions stemming from five complaints filed during the 2024 election: (A) adopt the CLIP-drafted language, (B) rely on existing state statutes and corrective actions already taken, or (C) work with the attorney to refine the ordinance. Trustee Coyle moved for Option C with a public hearing; Trustee Lesniak seconded. After extended debate about the risks of mirroring state statutes in local ordinance and the need to avoid ongoing maintenance issues, Trustee Coyle withdrew the motion. The board ultimately directed Clerk Jennifer to draft internal policy guidelines incorporating corrective actions and aligned with state statute, then bring the result back to CLIP for review. Trustee Myszka noted a specific technical concern with Section 41-3 regarding alternates language that should be updated.

Clerk Jennifer presented the proposal citing U.S. Postal Service delays causing some residents to miss ballot return deadlines. The board debated the need for surveillance cameras on the box; it was ultimately agreed that a camera would not be installed initially. Trustee Stowell moved to approve the drop box for the August 2026 primary; Trustee Lesniak seconded. The motion was then amended by Trustee Stowell to include both the August primary and November general election, with a report back to the board on usage and any damage. The amended motion passed unanimously on a voice vote. Lieutenant Smart was asked to inform the department to monitor the drop box, noting that tampering could carry misdemeanor or felony charges under Wisconsin law.

President Joling brought the item forward after receiving ongoing correspondence from a resident demanding enforcement against a neighbor's tree. Greg (public works) explained that the village has effectively limited its involvement to trees in the right-of-way since grant funding dried up. Trustee Coyle argued the ordinance should be removed entirely and replaced with a website guideline since there is no funding or staff to enforce it. Others, including Trustee Solheim and President Joling, favored updating rather than repealing the ordinance and working cooperatively with residents. The board directed staff to review and update the oak wilt ordinance and bring it back through CLIP, while also asking that a resource list of local arborists and DNR links be posted on the village website.

Administrator Dave and Greg presented details on the six-bay equipment garage project, explaining that a firewall between the police and DPW sections necessitated the addition of a second restroom on the police side to avoid the cost of a three-hour-rated fire door (estimated $7,000–$10,000). The restroom addition brings the total bid from the originally approved $799,000 to $814,815. Trustee Coyle made the motion to approve the amended bid; Trustee Myszka seconded. The board voted 7-0 to approve.

Trustee Lesniak moved and Trustee Stowell seconded a motion to convene in closed session pursuant to Wisconsin Statutes 19.85(1)(b) for consideration of dismissal, discipline, or investigation of charges against a public employee, and pursuant to Wisconsin Public Records Law. The roll call vote was 7-0 in favor.

discussions.item: Acknowledge June 2026 Water and Sewer Month
discussions.body: A motion was made and seconded to acknowledge June 2026 as Water and Sewer Month. The motion passed unanimously on a voice vote with no discussion.

Staff member Michael provided updates on multiple active projects. Western Avenue patch paving is largely complete with two rough patches remaining and two inoperable hydrants to be repaired. Scoffield Avenue specialty pavement markings and concrete work remain outstanding. Alderson Street and Jelnik concrete work is beginning and the intersection is expected to open around the first week of August, before school starts. Bladel Avenue reconstruction is roughly two-thirds complete on water main and sanitary sewer, with an early October finish date on schedule. The committee discussed the Rothschild/Bellwood project delay, with Rothschild reallocating funds to repave Eagles Nest Boulevard instead, pushing the shared project to next year. The DOT is reviewing Business 51 storm pond modeling; staff noted DOT contributes roughly 15% of the phosphorus load, equating to approximately $450,000 of a $3 million project, and a response is needed by end of month.

Staff reported that rural ditch and right-of-way mowing has begun along Scoffield Avenue, Camp Phillips, and other corridors. Shouldering on Shorry Avenue from Camp Phillips to Anastasia took a crew of eight about a day and a half. Excavation on Shirley Street is underway, stripping blacktop and removing clay/organic subgrade material, replacing it with approximately two to three feet of sand fill and 12 inches of recycled base; about 300 feet remain of the 1,300-foot project. Norcon completed repairs on Scoffield Avenue, fixing close to 200 failing panels from Esther to Tegan Street. Norcon also completed bridge deck repairs on Ross Avenue over the Eau Claire River in two days; the committee noted the deck is deteriorating and discussed that repairs are a temporary fix, with a full bridge replacement discussion deferred to Item 14. Farner Asphalt is performing crack sealing but postponed chip sealing of the Sandy Lane roundabout due to heat and humidity concerns.

Utility director Josh reported that unidirectional water main flushing is ongoing, currently near the Alderson/Radkey area, requiring about 10 to 12 weeks to complete the whole village and flushing approximately 12 to 15 million gallons annually. Josh noted a utility operator gave notice and is leaving, reducing the team from five to four operators; a job posting will go out shortly. The SCADA system is fully operational with minor interface fine-tuning ongoing; staff are developing a wish list of additional features. InPipe Technologies will begin an inflow and infiltration study in the annexed area near Wall Street at the end of the month, with a manhole rehabilitation project expected to be ready for award next month. A pump was pulled due to a wipes clog, prompting discussion of issuing public notices about flushing only appropriate materials.

Staff received four survey proposals for the 2027 Howland Avenue reconstruction project. Point of Beginning submitted the low bid of $12,500 with a four-to-five-week turnaround; Breland Associates offered the fastest three-week schedule. Staff recommended Point of Beginning on cost since schedule was not a primary concern. A committee member moved to award the surveying contract to Point of Beginning at $12,500 and the motion passed unanimously on a voice vote.

Michael presented a village-wide street light map showing existing lights (red dots), unlit intersections (yellow), and unlit road bends (green). Following the minimum policy standard of lights at intersections, dead ends, bends, and every tenth mile would require approximately 121 additional lights at an upfront cost of roughly $250,000 and an annual operating increase of about $33,000. A committee member raised Ross Avenue as a safety concern due to frequent deer strikes in the dark corridor parallel to the Eau Claire River. The committee agreed staff should obtain a WPS quote for spacing lights along Ross Avenue from Camp Phillips to the river, and should consult the police department for data on accident and deer strike locations before any broader decisions. Members expressed opposition to a blanket village-wide lighting policy, preferring targeted improvements in high-traffic or high-risk areas. No vote was taken; staff was directed to get a WPS quote and police input.

Four bids were received for the Concord Avenue and Bayberry Street reconstruction project: HS Suns at $2,223,819.90 (low bid), PGA at approximately $2,241,000, A1 at $2.36 million, and Integrity at $2.567 million. Staff recommended HS Suns, noting they have performed satisfactorily on multiple recent village projects including Jelnik Avenue, Scoffield Avenue, and the current roundabout. An alternate bid of $25,000 from HS Suns for a sidewalk connection in the Aspen area was also discussed; the committee agreed it was more cost-effective to include it now rather than return later. A committee member moved to award the project to HS Suns including the alternate for a total of $2,248,819.90 (base $2,223,819.90 plus alternate $25,000 approximately); the motion was seconded and passed unanimously on a voice vote.

Staff outlined several major upcoming projects for 2027–2030 and beyond. The Ross Avenue bridge over the Eau Claire River, built in 1979, is deteriorating rapidly with a hollow-sounding deck on chain testing; the committee agreed staff should develop an RFP for a structural analysis and bridge design consultation as soon as possible, noting the DOT permitting process could take four to five years. PFAS treatment was flagged as a pressing water utility need, with the Bladel and Alta Verde wells creeping toward the EPA recommended level of four parts per trillion; staff proposed designing treatment plants at those wells and pursuing DNR safe drinking water loan funding. The Fox Street lift station was identified as the oldest and most vulnerable lift station, with a small wet well and recent near-failures. Water and sewer master plans from 2017–2018 are due for a 10-year update. The Camp Phillips corridor (County Road X) was discussed; the county highway commissioner envisions an engineering study in 2028–2029 and noted the corridor is nearing traffic capacity with no practical reconstruction within its current footprint. Asbestos cement water main replacement was raised as a topic for a future meeting, with committee members urging pursuit of grant funding to accelerate the estimated 10-plus-year replacement timeline. Mountain Bay Metro Police Department evidence storage was noted as now moved out of the public safety building main structure to the two outbuildings. The Mountain Bay Metro Police Department building bid opening was noted for Thursday at 10:00 a.m.

overview: The Village of Kronenwetter's CLIPP Committee met on July 6, 2026, conducting a public hearing on revisions to Chapter 382 (Nuisances) of the village code and unanimously voting to forward the updated ordinance language to the Village Board for approval. The committee also discussed a traffic study recommendation for the County Road XX and Terabonding Drive intersection and heard a public comment requesting a bike and pedestrian path along Highway X.

discussions.body: Village President Dan Joling provided an overview of the proposed changes, explaining the ordinance removes the word 'public' from 'public nuisance' to make it more legally enforceable, requires complaints to be verified by law enforcement or supported by quantifiable evidence to prevent neighbor disputes, and extends the abatement period from 24 to 48 hours. Police Chief Terry McHugh confirmed the ordinance is largely similar to existing language with wordsmithing changes. No members of the public offered comment during the hearing.

discussions.item: Public Comment - Highway X Bike and Pedestrian Path
discussions.body: Kim Mayer, a resident near the intersection of Highway X and Pleasant Drive, presented a seven-page petition with signatures collected door-to-door and at the YMCA, advocating for a dedicated bike and pedestrian path along Highway X from Holland Avenue at the YMCA south to the intersection of Highway X and Highway XX. She cited safety concerns for children on scooters, cyclists, and pedestrians sharing the road with fast-moving traffic, and noted that both Police Chief McHugh and County Highway Commissioner Kevin Lane expressed support, with Lane indicating grant money is available. Committee members asked clarifying questions about the route and indicated staff would research costs and grant options for a future agenda.

discussions.body: A motion was made by Patty [Tikowski] to accept the June 1 CLIPP meeting minutes, seconded by Paul [Mayjol]. The committee approved the minutes by voice vote with no opposition.

Chief McHugh reported that calls for service are on pace to reach 8,000 in 2026, up from 7,100 the prior year, with an uptick in disturbances, fights, and drug-related incidents. He noted that following Officer Don's resignation, the department accelerated hiring: a new officer with prior law enforcement experience completed field training early and will soon begin solo patrol, a second hire's background process has been expedited with a target start of next month, and a third position has been posted on Wilinget with interviews planned for August and a fall hire anticipated.

Public Works Director Greg reported that the new maintenance shed is expected to have concrete poured in August with completion by January. He noted that state legislation raised the public bidding threshold, which is beneficial given rising costs. Sanitary sewer flow remains elevated at approximately 400,000 gallons per day due to a wet spring and early summer, down from higher levels but still above the target of 300,000. He also noted road salt prices increased about $17 per ton from the state contract.

discussions.item: Chapter 382 Nuisances - Vote to Forward to Village Board
discussions.body: Following the public hearing with no public opposition, Garrett Lizney moved to pass the revised nuisance ordinance language to the Village Board for approval. The motion was seconded and passed unanimously on a 5-0 roll call vote with all members voting yes.

discussions.item: Traffic Control - County Road XX and Terabonding Drive
discussions.body: Public Works Director Greg explained that County Highway Commissioner Kevin Lane requested elected officials' input on whether to make the current temporary four-way stop at County Road XX and Terabonding Drive permanent. Staff recommended commissioning a traffic study before making a decision rather than either immediately supporting or opposing a permanent four-way stop. The committee reached consensus to recommend the county conduct a traffic study while keeping the four-way stop in place during the study period, and that recommendation will be forwarded to the county.

overview: The Village of Kronenwetter held its inaugural Parks Committee meeting on June 29, 2026, electing officers, reviewing committee duties, and launching into substantive planning for Bushka Park improvements and fundraising. The newly formed seven-member committee — two trustees and five citizen members — focused heavily on a roughly $150,000-$200,000 playground replacement project at Bushka Park, with a public fundraiser planned for a July 17 movie-under-the-stars event. The committee also scheduled a parks tour for Wednesday, July 8 at 4 p.m. and set a meeting cadence of the first and third Mondays of July and August at 4 p.m.

discussions.body: Patty DeCaliskey nominated Trustee Erin Mishka for chairperson. No other nominations were offered. A voice vote was taken; the ayes carried with one abstention noted. Erin Mishka was elected chairperson and assumed the chair for the remainder of the meeting.

Patty DeCaliskey nominated Dan Lesniac for vice chairperson. A roll call vote was taken; Theresa Holowinsky, Dan Lesniac, Tim Stracota, Patty DeCaliskey, Elizabeth Vedvik, and Trustee Mishka all voted yes. The motion carried unanimously.

Jennifer Poirier reviewed the committee's governing ordinances, noting the seven-member composition, four-member quorum requirement, advisory-only role to the Village Board, and the committee's duration of up to one year expiring at end of April. Trustee Mishka was credited with developing the duties document. Mishka indicated she would forgo her committee pay so the budget could support a potential sixth meeting.

The committee discussed the recently completed outdoor recreation plan, with Chairperson Mishka highlighting that the plan's core recommendations begin on page 36 and cover all village parks. Members noted a survey of only 156 respondents out of 8,623 residents felt too narrow in scope. Dan Lesniac shared anecdotal evidence of Bushka Park's baseball field being used daily. The committee agreed the plan should serve as a guiding document while also gathering additional community input, and that Bushka Park playground replacement — already identified as a top priority — aligns with survey findings that updated equipment was residents' top concern.

discussions.item: Bushka Park Fundraiser (Movie Under the Stars / July 17 Event)
discussions.body: The committee discussed leveraging the July 17 movie-under-the-stars event, hosted annually by On Cue Solutions (Ronda), as a fundraising kickoff for the Bushka Park playground project. The current fundraising balance is approximately $5,000 toward a goal of $200,000, with the base playground quote from Lee's Recreation at approximately $150,000, and the higher goal intended to allow for a rubberized surface instead of ADA wood chips. Ideas discussed included a wishing-well style transparent pool for coin/cash donations with QR code cards, Patty DeCaliskey selling jewelry with a portion going to the park, Elizabeth Vedvik doing home-bakery sales, a potential 50/50 raffle through On Cue Solutions (who holds a raffle license), a large presentation on the movie screen showing equipment breakdowns and sponsorship levels, and potential naming rights for playground elements such as swings or slides. The committee discussed the need to develop formal donation tiers with recognition (e.g., plaques). Chairperson Mishka and Vice Chair Lesniac noted they would both be absent July 17; Patty DeCaliskey and others agreed to present the fundraising pitch.

The committee brainstormed a wide range of future fundraising concepts including a 5K run/walk or poker walk connecting village parks, a summer concert event at Towering Pines Park with food trucks and a beer tent, a fall block party potentially in partnership with Relocation bar (which holds a liquor license), a carnival-style event with kids' games, and partnering with the Lion's Club on a fall fest. Members also discussed adding a park fundraising component to National Night Out (August 4) including a tug-of-war between police and fire departments. Jennifer Poirier noted the village cannot independently hold a raffle without partnering with a licensed organization. The committee agreed to focus near-term energy on the July 17 event and an August concert event, tentatively discussed for around August 23.

The committee agreed to conduct a parks tour led by Village Administrator Greg, planned for Wednesday, July 8 at 4 p.m. meeting at the municipal center, with Thursday, July 9 at 4 p.m. as a rain date. The tour will cover approximately five parks, with the committee debating whether to visit all parks; leadership recommended focusing on the busiest five parcels first to avoid exhaustion, with additional park visits possible at future meetings. The tour will be open to community members.

discussions.body: The committee agreed to meet on the first and third Mondays of July and August at 4 p.m., mirroring the schedule of the clip committee and plan commission. Specific dates discussed were July 20, August 3, and August 17. Members noted that once the school year begins, Monday afternoon meetings would become difficult; the committee aimed to complete most of its work by end of August. Additional meetings could be added as needed on alternate days such as Thursdays.

title: City Council Retreat Meeting Pt.2
overview: The Wausau City Council held a strategic planning retreat where council members shared their top priorities for the 2026-2028 term, focusing heavily on economic development, housing affordability, fleet facility construction, transit expansion, and youth retention. The meeting concluded with a motion, passed unanimously, directing staff coordinator Michelle to compile all priority input from sticky notes and dot-voting exercises into a digestible format for distribution by end of week, after which the council will formally act on identifying the top three priorities.

discussions.body: Alderman Myers and Alder Trueblood both strongly advocated for action on the fleet facility, with Trueblood noting he has been on council eight years and the issue has been discussed for six of them with no resolution. A former infrastructure committee member noted the city has already spent $100,000-$200,000 on building plans and that much legwork is done, offering to attend future meetings to provide history on the project. The consensus among speakers was that the fleet facility must be completed this term rather than waiting for a potential county site to open up.

Alder Neal delivered an extended argument that council members and the public fundamentally misunderstand TIF and TID tools, warning that characterizing developer incentives as 'taxpayer money going to rich people' is inaccurate and puts Wausau at a competitive disadvantage. Alder Kilian countered that high market-rate rents in new apartment buildings are unaffordable for workers earning $20-$22 per hour, and called for more education so residents understand how these projects are financed. Alder Trueblood advocated for housing at all levels including market rate, affordable, single-family, duplexes, and accessory dwelling units, noting Wausau's housing stock is old and land for expansion is limited. Mayor Diny noted that developers build what generates ROI and the city's role is to work with developers, not act as one.

Alder Neal argued forcefully that attracting and retaining youth should be a top-line strategic priority, stating 'if we don't have a plan and if we aren't actively doing everything we can to attract and retain our youth here, our schools are emptying out.' He noted Wausau school enrollment has declined from roughly 8,400 to 7,400 students since 2000. Alder Tierney raised the idea of things for teens to do that don't cost money and mentioned reviving a mayor's youth council. Mayor Diny referenced Bentonville, Arkansas as a model community that transformed itself into a destination through trail systems and amenities, reversing talent drain.

One alder raised the issue of profound civic disengagement, noting that council and committee meetings routinely have empty houses, YouTube analytics on city meetings are very low, and the city lacks a centralized, cohesive communication strategy across departments. Alder Kilian described success with a neighborhood group in her district that now draws a packed room monthly. Multiple council members discussed the need for plain-language videos explaining tax bills and budget, with one alder describing spending hours with city staff to understand the revaluation before being able to explain it to constituents.

Alder Trueblood called Metro Ride the one thing Wausau has that no other community has and said it must be leveraged. Mayor Diny noted new transit director Ron Schunky is taking a new approach to regional expansion—selling transit to neighboring communities based on benefit to them rather than cost—and cited a new Northern Valley route serving 40-plus riders per day as early progress. Alder Luken advocated for expanding public transportation routes and times to serve residents who cannot afford personal vehicles, particularly to connect workers to local and regional employers.

Alder Tierney raised the issue of Wausau taxpayers funding police and ambulance overtime for county-wide events such as the fair, Art in the Park, and the upcoming air show, and suggested Marathon County share those costs. Another alder responded that the overtime issue is more nuanced than it appears, citing meetings held with the mayor, police chief, fire chief, and DPW, and announced an HR committee meeting on July 13th where all department heads will be invited to address overtime on the record. Council members were invited to submit questions in advance.

Alder Tierney raised the lack of public follow-up on the city's PFAS lawsuits, noting residents don't know what settlement money has been received or how it's being used. The city attorney confirmed payments have been received from 3M, Tyco, BASF, and DuPont over a settlement structure that will continue for nine years, and that a special needs claim is still pending for this summer. The attorney stated no settlement money has been allocated to anything yet and committed to preparing a confidential litigation summary update. Council members requested a finance department accounting of how funds are tracked.

The motion was seconded and passed unanimously with no opposition.

overview: The Wausau School Board Committee of the Whole met on June 22, 2026, approving several action items including Wisconsin Academic Standards for the 2026-27 school year, WIAA membership renewals, a $420,000 EFIS wall replacement contract at South Mountain Elementary, and authorization to use equipment auction proceeds for buildings and grounds equipment purchases. The board also received an informational AGR schools data presentation showing generally positive trends in math and literacy outcomes, and recognized the retirement of a 32-year district employee.

discussions.body: Miss Channel announced the retirement of Nol Torson after 32 years with the Wausau School District, expressing pride in his service. She also announced that Jen Bonnke would be taking his position as supervisor of financial services. The board chair noted Torson is a quiet individual and did not put him on the spot to speak.
The board was asked to approve the audit of bills as presented. A motion was made, seconded, and passed unanimously with no discussion or public comment.

discussions.item: Annual Adoption of Wisconsin Academic Standards for 2026-27
discussions.body: Dr. Katie Cowwell and Miss Shell presented the annual notice, explaining the standards were created in 1988 and that Wisconsin Act 55 (2015) requires annual board approval. They noted DPI plans to review standards for dance, art, world languages, and environmental literacy this fall, and that there are now 25 content standards including new additions for art and design and WIDA English language development. The motion to approve passed unanimously.
The board considered annual renewal of WIAA memberships for Wausau East, Wausau West, and WAVE. No questions were raised. The motion to recommend approval to the full board passed unanimously.

A large team including district administrators, literacy coordinator Sandy, and building principals Jen Davidson (JD Jones), Phil Beckham (JD Jones associate principal), and Matt Schilling (Thomas Jefferson associate principal) presented spring data for Franklin, JD Jones, and Thomas Jefferson elementary schools. Math scores showed a slow uphill trajectory since fall 2023-24 with AGR buildings at approximately 62-64% at benchmark; kindergarten and first grade showed strong gains using the new Forefront number sense screener in its first year of use. Literacy data showed improvement over the prior year though some grade levels showed slight declines. Board member discussion focused heavily on classroom management after a board member shared a story of a newer teacher who didn't know she was empowered to firmly address disruptive behavior; administrators confirmed professional development on classroom management is planned including on the first day back. Board members also questioned assessment overload and spring testing fatigue, with staff acknowledging assessment windows would be adjusted. This item was informational only with no action taken.

discussions.item: South Mountain Elementary EFIS Wall System Replacement
discussions.body: Buildings and Grounds Director Ryan Hermansky presented the need to replace the EFIS (stucco) wall system at South Mountain Elementary, citing design defects identified through engineering assessment. He recommended replacing the system with 20-gauge steel panels, the same approach successfully used at Horace Mann last fall. Four bids were received and Jackson Associates, who also completed the Horace Mann project, was the low bidder at $420,000 with work planned for November 2026. A board member asked whether Jackson was responsible for the original faulty installation; Hermansky clarified Jackson did the repair work at Horace Mann, not the original installation. The motion to recommend full board approval of the bid and contract passed unanimously.

discussions.item: District Equipment Auction and Proceeds Designation
discussions.body: Hermansky requested board approval to hold an online auction through Wisconsin Surplus of obsolete district equipment including old lawnmowers, an automated mower blade sharpener, and a log splitter, and to direct the proceeds back to buildings and grounds for equipment purchases rather than the general fund. He estimated proceeds of $30,000-$60,000. A board member asked about consolidated school furniture; Hermansky clarified most was redistributed to schools or disposed of. The motion to recommend full board approval for auction proceeds to be designated to buildings and grounds for 2026-27 equipment needs passed unanimously.

A special meeting was called immediately following adjournment of the Committee of the Whole. The consent agenda covering appointments, additional staff, replacement staff, contract increases, separations, resignations, contract decreases, terminations, leaves of absence, and retirements was approved unanimously without discussion.

overview: The Wausau Transit Commission met on June 18, 2026, and approved two key items: sending a WisGo electronic fare collection contract to the Finance Committee for review, and allowing transit buses to serve as crowd barriers at the Wings Over Wausau airshow. The meeting also featured public comment from a former commissioner, Kathy Flurry, who disputed her removal from the commission by Mayor Doug Diny, and heard a director's update on ongoing technology upgrades including a new CAD/AVL system and the hire of a new deputy director.
